titleStmt.title: Which Cognitive Abilities Make the Difference? Predicting Academic Achievements in Advanced STEM Studies
titleStmt.author: Berkowitz
Stern

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Which Cognitive Abilities Make the Difference? Predicting Academic Achievements in Advanced STEM Studies

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Ability differences within an already-selected group of STEM undergraduates, and which of those differences predict which first-year grades.
span.quote: We investigated whether ability differences among students who entered higher STEM education were predictive of achievements during the first undergraduate year.

span.label: prediction
span.quote: Math and physics achievements were best predicted by numerical, verbal and general reasoning abilities.

span.label: spatial ability as a predictor of STEM achievement
span.quote: We were concerned with the interplay between cognitive abilities and success in specific topics during higher STEM education, and particularly with the role of SA.

span.label: prospective-cohort-study
span.quote: In a prospective cohort design, we assessed students from two STEM programs on multiple measures of SV, numerical and verbal reasoning abilities.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Advanced mathematics is carried out by translating spatial structures into abstract symbolic formalism rather than by visualizing them, so exceptional visualization ability adds nothing to math achievement
span.quote: Math courses may focus on translating complex spatial structures into abstract mathematical formalism, more than they require superb visualization of such structures.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Where spatial tests do correlate with math grades, the link runs through domain-general reasoning components embedded in those tests rather than through visualization itself
span.quote: Additionally, our finding that positive correlations between one type of SV tests (visualization of cross-sections) and some math achievements were mediated by factors common to other domains of reasoning suggests that factors other than visualization—which may be strongly present in some spatial tests—play a role when it comes to mathematics.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Higher prior domain knowledge in self-selected STEM entrants removes the need to recruit spatial ability, weakening the SV-physics link
span.quote: One possible explanation for these differences is that students in our sample may have had higher levels of prior-knowledge in science: first at entry level due to self-selection, and at the time of achievements assessment (i.e., course exams), as it reflected learning during an entire academic year.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Application-oriented versus proof-oriented teaching of the same mathematical content recruits different abilities (calculation efficiency vs. broader reasoning)
span.quote: For example, application-oriented mathematics may require high efficiency in utilizing domain-specific skills and knowledge, which may explain the almost exclusive relation between numerical reasoning ability and math in the engineering group.

span.label: Prediction is domain specific on both sides: the ability that matters depends on what the course actually demands
span.quote: Thus, the predictions seem highly domain specific: differences in SV, even among the spatially talented, mattered when complex spatial tasks were in focus (technical drawing), whereas differences in numerical or verbal reasoning abilities among the mathematically talented mattered when math was in focus.

span.label: The proposed reading of the null: spatial ability has a threshold for mathematics that these students have already passed, so further differences buy nothing
span.quote: Apparently, when it comes to predicting mathematics achievements, SV seems to have a lower threshold than numerical and verbal abilities (i.e., a lower level is sufficient for success).

span.label: Spatial tests are not purely spatial - performance on them depends on executive function and on analytic strategies that do as well as visualising
span.quote: For example, Miyake et al. [ 31 ] showed that performance on SA tests, and particularly on SV tests, highly depended on executive functions, whereas others found that analytical- and heuristic-based strategies are as common and at least as efficient as visualization per se, sometimes even preferable [ 9 , 30 , 32 , 33 ].

span.label: Separating domain-specific from domain-general variance weakens some effects and strengthens the general factor, so how the model is specified changes which story it tells
span.quote: However, when specific effects were estimated from the residual variances of the specific abilities (as in model B), some of these effects became weaker, and the direct effects of the general factor became stronger.

span.label: In a high-ability sample the abilities overlap less than usual, which limits how much prediction is available to find
span.quote: It should be noted that the overlap between specific abilities in our sample was likely lower than in more heterogeneous samples (this is often found in high-ability groups [ 67 ]), possibly limiting its predictive power.

span.label: The study is small-scale, so generalisation to the wider STEM undergraduate population is not yet established.
span.quote: The present study was not a large-scale one, therefore generalizations to the population of STEM undergraduates are yet to be shown.

span.label: Restriction of range in spatial visualisation cannot be ruled out as a cause of the null spatial-math correlations.
span.quote: One may suspect that the lack of correlations between SV and math-based achievements is a result of a restriction of range in SV, and that in more heterogeneous samples positive correlations would emerge.

span.label: Too few women were sampled to draw conclusions about whether the findings apply to high-ability women.
span.quote: Nonetheless, since the number of women in our sample was too small for drawing strong conclusions, we think that future research is needed in order to clarify whether the current results apply to high-ability women in advanced STEM education.

span.label: Only two STEM disciplines were studied, a partial selection of the category.
span.quote: Finally, we focused on two major STEM disciplines, but this is still only a partial selection out of the variety of disciplines in this category.

span.label: Not a large-scale study, so generalisation to STEM undergraduates at large is not established
span.quote: The present study was not a large-scale one, therefore generalizations to the population of STEM undergraduates are yet to be shown.

span.label: The tests were too easy for this sample, compressing exactly the differences the design depends on
span.quote: Ideally, using tests that are more challenging in these populations would yield larger ability differences and thus enable further exploration of their impact.

span.label: The comparison literature is largely American, where students choose a major later, so 'STEM beginner' does not mean the same thing
span.quote: For example, in the U.S., students choose their major at a later point in their undergraduate studies comparing to Europe and other parts of the world, where they enroll on a particular program from the start.

span.label: Too few women to support conclusions about them, which the authors say plainly while reporting the pattern anyway
span.quote: Nonetheless, since the number of women in our sample was too small for drawing strong conclusions, we think that future research is needed in order to clarify whether the current results apply to high-ability women in advanced STEM education.

span.label: The study was aimed at students who select advanced STEM programs and is not offered as a claim about STEM learning generally
span.quote: Our study was therefore a-priori targeted at students who select advanced STEM programs rather than at generalizing to math and STEM learning more broadly.

span.label: SEVERAL different ability measures included rather than one
span.quote: we included multiple ability measures in order to ensure that the results are not dependent on a particular type of ability test

span.label: spatial ability (SA) - the broad literature term, used loosely and often for measures that are actually narrower
span.quote: Very broadly, spatial ability (SA) refers to “the ability to generate, retain, and manipulate abstract visual images” [ 19 ].

span.label: spatial visualization (SV) - the specific factor measured here, and the authors' stated convention is to say SV for their own work and SA when reporting prior research
span.quote: Since previous studies have often used the broad term SA even when measures were of SV, we use the term SA when referring to previous research in this field.

span.label: threshold - the general claim: above some ability level, further differences stop predicting anything
span.quote: Overall, our data clearly showed that ability differences in this high-ability population are relevant to achievement prediction, corroborating previous findings against a ‘threshold’ view of cognitive abilities [ 34 , 44 , 48 , 49 ].

span.label: threshold - per ability and per domain: each ability has its own level that suffices for a given subject, and spatial ability's is low for mathematics
span.quote: Apparently, when it comes to predicting mathematics achievements, SV seems to have a lower threshold than numerical and verbal abilities (i.e., a lower level is sufficient for success).

span.label: what a spatial test measures - as named: spatial-visual processing
span.quote: The most studied type of SA in the context of STEM is spatial visualization (SV), which is the ability to “…apprehend a spatial form, shape or scene in order to match it with another spatial form, shape or scene, often with the necessity of rotating it in two or three dimensions one or more times” [ 24 ].

span.label: what a spatial test measures - in practice: also executive function, and analytic strategies that substitute for visualising altogether
span.quote: Research showed that solving SA tests involves not only strictly spatial-visual processes, but also a variety of non-spatial components.

span.label: contradicts → Lubinski and Benbow (2006)
span.quote: Our results seem inconsistent with findings on the unique predictive validity of SA among students of extremely high ability (e.g., the top 0.01% in Lubinski and Benbow, 2006).

span.label: builds-on → Uttal and Cohen [16]
span.quote: As suggested by Uttal and Cohen [ 16 ], SA may be particularly important when domain-knowledge is low.

span.label: replicates → Miller and Halpern [44]
span.quote: Miller and Halpern [ 44 ] found positive effects of SA training on physics but not math grades of high-ability STEM students, and concluded that SA training was not relevant to the content of math courses, which is consistent with our own conclusion.

span.label: critiques → the threshold view that cognitive abilities stop predicting within highly selected samples
span.quote: Overall, our data clearly showed that ability differences in this high-ability population are relevant to achievement prediction, corroborating previous findings against a ‘threshold’ view of cognitive abilities [ 34 , 44 , 48 , 49 ].

span.label: critiques → the assumption that spatial ability is a broad predictor of STEM success during the novice phase
span.quote: It therefore appears that rather than broadly determining STEM success during the novice phase, as would be expected based on prior research assumptions, SV emerged as a narrower STEM predictor relative to other abilities, which in turn predicted success on a broader range of core STEM subjects.

span.label: extends → Carroll's broad definition of spatial visualisation, adopted here as the working sense
span.quote: We use the term SV in the broader sense suggested by Carroll [ 24 ], namely referring to complex mental manipulations of objects, mostly in three dimensions, involving either rotation or other forms of transformation.

span.label: critiques → the argument linking women's underrepresentation in STEM to their poorer spatial test performance
span.quote: Although it is beyond the scope of this study to directly address this issue, the possibility that high spatial skills are not crucial for higher mathematics puts in a different light the often-made arguments linking women’s poorer performance in SA tests to this gender gap.

span.label: spatial visualization —is-a→ spatial ability
span.quote: In fact, several types of SA have been identified since the early factor analytic studies on human cognitive abilities [ 20 , 21 ], and the exact distinctions vary between studies and theoretical frameworks [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ].

span.label: mental rotation —distinct-from→ spatial visualization
span.quote: Others have differentiated mental rotation from SV [ 25 ], defining the former as involving an analogue and holistic mental process and the latter as involving more complex, multistep mental manipulations.

span.label: spatial visualization —causes→ technical drawing
span.quote: In contrast, SV had unique predictive validity for achievements on an engineering technical drawing course.

span.label: numerical reasoning —causes→ STEM
span.quote: Moreover, numerical and verbal reasoning abilities were uniquely predictive of achievements on most math and physics courses.

span.label: spatial visualization —distinct-from→ STEM
span.quote: Across ability measures and study programs, SV did not uniquely predict achievements in math-intensive courses, which constitute a major part of the curriculum.

span.label: executive functions —causes→ spatial visualization
span.note: status: ATTRIBUTED, AND CONTRADICTED IN THE SAME SENTENCE: 'MIYAKE ET AL. [31] SHOWED that performance on SA tests, and particularly on SV tests, highly depended on executive functions, WHEREAS OTHERS FOUND that analytical- and heuristic-based strategies are as common and at least as efficient as visualization'. The edge carries Miyake et al.'s finding, which is real; the same span carries the opposing position, and a reader joining on the edge alone gets one side of a live disagreement.
span.quote: For example, Miyake et al. [ 31 ] showed that performance on SA tests, and particularly on SV tests, highly depended on executive functions, whereas others found that analytical- and heuristic-based strategies are as common and at least as efficient as visualization per se, sometimes even preferable [ 9 , 30 , 32 , 33 ].

span.label: Paper Folding Test —operationalised-as→ spatial visualization
span.quote: Typical tests reflecting this factor are The Paper Folding Test [ 27 ] and The Mental Rotations Test [ 28 , 29 ].

span.label: Mental Rotations Test —operationalised-as→ mental rotation
span.quote: Typical tests reflecting this factor are The Paper Folding Test [ 27 ] and The Mental Rotations Test [ 28 , 29 ].

span.label: latent ability factors —part-of→ structural equation model
span.quote: In a structural equation model, we estimated the effects of latent ability factors on students’ achievements on a range of first year courses.

span.label: domain-general —contrasted-with→ domain specific
span.quote: Taken together, isolating domain-specific from domain-general effects still showed strong domain-specific effects in both of the groups, but in some cases domain-general factors clearly contributed to the prediction.

span.label: threshold —causes→ spatial visualization
span.quote: When it comes to advanced STEM learning, different thresholds may exist for different disciplines.

span.label: SA training —operationalised-as→ spatial ability
span.quote: Evidence has also accumulated supporting the utility of SA training, which is regarded as a potentially efficient way to increase young students’ chances of entering and remaining in STEM domains [ 14 , 15 ].

span.label: general reasoning —operationalised-as→ domain-general
span.quote: That is, most of the effects of specific abilities remained significant beyond a general ability factor.

span.label: structural equation modeling
span.quote: The effects of abilities on academic achievements were then estimated in a structural equation model (SEM).

span.label: maximum likelihood estimation (robust)
span.quote: In all analyses, robust maximum likelihood estimation (MLR) was used, which takes into account non-normal distributions.

span.label: root mean square error of approximation
span.term: root mean square error of approximation
span.quote: Approximate fit indices: (2) Steiger-Lind Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA); [ 52 ], and its 90% confidence interval (3) Bentler Comparative Fit Index (CFI); [ 53 ] (4) Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR).

span.label: comparative fit index
span.quote: Approximate fit indices: (2) Steiger-Lind Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA); [ 52 ], and its 90% confidence interval (3) Bentler Comparative Fit Index (CFI); [ 53 ] (4) Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR).

span.label: standardized root mean square residual
span.quote: Approximate fit indices: (2) Steiger-Lind Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA); [ 52 ], and its 90% confidence interval (3) Bentler Comparative Fit Index (CFI); [ 53 ] (4) Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR).

span.label: Cronbach's alpha
span.quote: For most scales, reliability estimates based on Cronbach’s alpha were within an acceptable range, though lower than in more heterogeneous samples.

span.label: greatest lower bound reliability
span.quote: We additionally report the general lower bound (GLB) estimate of scale reliability, which has been found to be a more accurate measure of reliability than the alpha coefficient in cases of skewed distributions [ 63 , 64 ].

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Independent samples t -tests (corrected for multiple comparisons) revealed a significant difference in favor of students with grades only on one measure (‘numerical signs’; t = 3.76, p < 0.001; d = 0.60).

span.label: effect size (Cohen's d)
span.quote: Independent samples t -tests (corrected for multiple comparisons) revealed small effect-size differences in favor of math-physics students on two measures: Schnitte (M = 8.01, SD = 2.78 in engineering; M = 9.06, SD = 3.18 in math-physics; t = 3.01, p = 0.003, d = 0.34); and verbal similarities (M = 12.07, SD = 2.61 in engineering; M = 13.11, SD = 2.41 in math-physics; t = 3.67, p < 0.001, d = 0.41).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: There were no significant differences between cohorts on age (F 2,314 = 0.19, p = 0.83), proportions in study programs (χ 2 = 4.29, p = 0.12) or proportion of women (χ 2 = 2.11, p = 0.35).

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: There were no significant differences between cohorts on age (F 2,314 = 0.19, p = 0.83), proportions in study programs (χ 2 = 4.29, p = 0.12) or proportion of women (χ 2 = 2.11, p = 0.35).

span.label: full information maximum likelihood (missing data)
span.quote: Full information maximum likelihood (FIML) was used for treating all missing data (the default in Mplus).

span.label: factor analysis (exploratory and confirmatory)
span.quote: Prior to estimating the relations between abilities and academic achievements, we conducted exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses in order to establish a model of cognitive abilities.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Table 5 and Table 6 present the observed correlations between cognitive measures and grades among engineering and math-physics students respectively (the full correlation matrices are included in the supplementary materials Section 1) .

span.label: Spatial ability uniquely predicted achievement in an engineering design course but not in mathematics or physics, once numerical, verbal and general reasoning were controlled.
span.quote: Although ability-test scores were mostly at the upper scale range, differential effects on achievements were found: spatial ability accounted for achievements in an engineering design course beyond numerical, verbal and general reasoning abilities, but not for math and physics achievements.

span.label: Numerical, verbal and general reasoning abilities were the best predictors of mathematics and physics grades.
span.quote: Math and physics achievements were best predicted by numerical, verbal and general reasoning abilities.

span.label: Among mechanical engineering students, spatial visualization showed no relation to mathematics or physics grades even at the zero-order (uncontrolled) level.
span.quote: In fact, SV was unrelated to the math and physics grades of engineering students even before controlling for other abilities.

span.label: Among math-physics students, spatial visualization correlated with grades but added no incremental prediction beyond the other ability factors.
span.quote: Among math-physics students, SV had no incremental predictive power for any of the grades.

span.label: The unique effect of numerical reasoning on math and physics grades held for engineering students but disappeared for math-physics students once other abilities were controlled.
span.quote: Among engineering students, numerical ability had strong unique effects on math and physics courses, whereas among math-physics students its effects were no longer significant once other abilities were controlled for.

span.label: Spatial visualization did survive as a predictor for the one explicitly spatial engineering course (technical drawing and CAD).
span.quote: SV remained a significant predictor of grades on a highly ‘spatial’ course in the engineering program (T.D.CAD).

span.label: Individual differences in cognitive ability still predicted achievement inside this highly selected, high-ability student sample, contradicting a threshold view.
span.quote: Overall, our data clearly showed that ability differences in this high-ability population are relevant to achievement prediction, corroborating previous findings against a ‘threshold’ view of cognitive abilities [ 34 , 44 , 48 , 49 ].

span.label: spatial visualisation did not uniquely predict achievement in math-intensive courses, which are most of the curriculum
span.quote: Across ability measures and study programs, SV did not uniquely predict achievements in math-intensive courses, which constitute a major part of the curriculum.

span.label: spatial visualisation was unrelated to engineering students' math and physics grades even before controlling for anything
span.quote: In fact, SV was unrelated to the math and physics grades of engineering students even before controlling for other abilities.

span.label: it did uniquely predict grades in technical drawing, the one explicitly spatial course
span.quote: In contrast, SV had unique predictive validity for achievements on an engineering technical drawing course.

span.label: numerical and verbal reasoning predicted most math and physics grades
span.quote: Moreover, numerical and verbal reasoning abilities were uniquely predictive of achievements on most math and physics courses.

span.label: ability differences still predicted achievement within an already highly selected sample, against the threshold view
span.quote: Overall, our data clearly showed that ability differences in this high-ability population are relevant to achievement prediction, corroborating previous findings against a ‘threshold’ view of cognitive abilities [ 34 , 44 , 48 , 49 ].

span.label: women scored lower on mental rotations yet did no worse in math-intensive courses, and mental rotation was unrelated to math grades in both groups
span.quote: Interestingly, even the highly competent women in our study tended to do worse than men in mental rotations, but there was no indication that women had less success in their math-intensive courses, and mental rotation was unrelated to math achievements across groups.

span.label: spatial ability (SA)
span.quote: Very broadly, spatial ability (SA) refers to “the ability to generate, retain, and manipulate abstract visual images” [ 19 ].

span.label: spatial visualization (SV)
span.quote: The most studied type of SA in the context of STEM is spatial visualization (SV), which is the ability to “…apprehend a spatial form, shape or scene in order to match it with another spatial form, shape or scene, often with the necessity of rotating it in two or three dimensions one or more times” [ 24 ].

span.label: threshold hypothesis (of cognitive ability)
span.quote: Since this population was likely to be a high-ability group due to factors such as self-selection and admission criteria, our investigation also challenged the notion that ability differences cease to matter in higher levels of performance (the so-called “threshold hypothesis” [ 47 ]).

span.label: spatial ability
span.quote: Very broadly, spatial ability (SA) refers to “the ability to generate, retain, and manipulate abstract visual images” [ 19 ].

span.label: spatial visualization
span.quote: the ability to “…apprehend a spatial form, shape or scene in order to match it with another spatial form, shape or scene, often with the necessity of rotating it in two or three dimensions one or more times”

span.label: mental rotation
span.quote: defining the former as involving an analogue and holistic mental process and the latter as involving more complex, multistep mental manipulations

span.label: spatial visualization (SV) ability
span.quote: Consistent with previous research, we focused our investigation on SV ability.

span.label: verbal reasoning ability (latent factor)
span.quote: Since our focus was on the interplay between specific abilities in achievement prediction (i.e., their unique predictive validity), we first specified a correlated factors model with three latent variables: verbal reasoning, numerical reasoning and spatial visualization (SV).

span.label: numerical reasoning ability (latent factor)
span.quote: Since our focus was on the interplay between specific abilities in achievement prediction (i.e., their unique predictive validity), we first specified a correlated factors model with three latent variables: verbal reasoning, numerical reasoning and spatial visualization (SV).

span.label: first-year course grades (academic achievement)
span.quote: Students’ grades on a range of first year courses served as measures of academic achievements and were based on scores in written exams.

span.label: general ability factor (g)
span.quote: To disentangle the effects of specific abilities from domain-general factors, we additionally tested models in which a general ability factor was included.

span.label: study program (mechanical engineering vs. math-physics)
span.quote: Math and physics students have an identical curriculum during the first undergraduate year and therefore formed one group in this study, while engineering students formed the second group.

span.label: spatial visualisation ability
span.quote: Our primary focus was on the particular role of SV ability for different STEM topics.

span.label: numerical and verbal reasoning ability
span.quote: Moreover, numerical and verbal reasoning abilities were uniquely predictive of achievements on most math and physics courses.

span.label: first-year course grades
span.quote: In a structural equation model, we estimated the effects of latent ability factors on students’ achievements on a range of first year courses.

span.label: general ability factor
span.quote: That is, most of the effects of specific abilities remained significant beyond a general ability factor.

span.label: study programme (engineering versus math-physics)
span.quote: Differently from other studies on advanced STEM learning, we systematically differentiated between ability domains, domains of achievements, study programs and ability measures.

span.label: 317 — final analysed sample of first-year undergraduates, split into 150 engineers and 167 math-physics students
span.quote: The final sample size was therefore 317, with 150 mechanical engineering students and 167 math-physics students.

span.label: 119.71 / 128.15 — sample mean IQ relative to high-school-graduate norms and to general-population norms, confirming a high-ability sample
span.quote: In general IQ scores, our sample had a mean IQ of 119.71 ( SD = 11.15) relative to the norms for high-school graduates, and 128.15 ( SD = 10.72) relative to the general population norms.

span.label: χ 2 /df = 95.42/50; RMSEA = 0.05; CFI = 0.94; SRMR = 0.05 — fit statistics of the retained three-correlated-factors measurement model of cognitive abilities
span.quote: Fit statistics for this model were as follows: χ 2 /df = 95.42/50, p ≤ 0.001; RMSEA (90% CI) = 0.05 (0.04–0.07); CFI = 0.94; SRMR = 0.05.

span.label: 150 — minimum observations per group the authors targeted, from prior simulations, to detect latent effects of about 0.3
span.quote: Prior simulation studies indicated that in order to detect effects of about 0.3 (latent level) with a correlated factors model (i.e., path coefficients from any ability factor to an outcome), a minimum of about 150 observations would be needed in each group.

span.label: 30% — failure rate on the first-year exams at ETH, used to argue the first year is critical for retention
span.quote: Finally, the first undergraduate year at ETH is a critical one for retention: students undergo challenging exams with a failure rate of 30%.

span.label: 44 (14%) — participants who did not sit final exams and therefore had missing grade data
span.quote: Finally, 44 participants (14% of the sample) did not attend final exams and therefore had missing data on grades.

span.label: 317 undergraduate students — the sample, split between two programmes
span.quote: We assessed 317 undergraduate students in Switzerland (150 from mechanical engineering and 167 from math-physics) on multiple measures of spatial, verbal and numerical abilities.

span.label: 150 from mechanical engineering and 167 from math-physics — the two study programmes compared throughout
span.quote: We assessed 317 undergraduate students in Switzerland (150 from mechanical engineering and 167 from math-physics) on multiple measures of spatial, verbal and numerical abilities.

span.label: the top 0.5% and 0.01% — the selectivity of the comparison studies, far above this sample
span.quote: The emphasis here was on ability differences within an expectedly high-ability sample of STEM undergraduates, yet not as selected as in other studies (e.g., the top 0.5% and 0.01% in [ 18 ]).

span.label: first 2–3 semesters — the novice window in which spatial ability was said to be critical
span.quote: For example, reviewing expert-novice studies in several domains, Uttal and Cohen [ 16 ] concluded that psychometrically assessed SA is critical for STEM novices (i.e., during the first 2–3 semesters as STEM majors), but becomes less critical with increasing expertise.
